problem: Existing embodied language benchmarks either give a single up-front instruction with no further communication and use planner-generated demonstrations (R2R, ALFRED), or support dialogue only for navigation, without object state changes, with enforced turn-taking and few sessions (CVDN, CerealBar, MDC). No large dataset combined free-form human–human dialogue with object interaction and state-changing household tasks.
motivation: Robots in homes must understand instructions and also use conversation to resolve ambiguity and correct mistakes. Prior work showed that clarification or dialogue history helps navigation, and the authors hypothesize dialogue helps even more for object-centric, hierarchical tasks. Human (not planner) demonstrations naturally contain mistakes, language-guided corrections, variable instruction granularity and interleaved (non-turn-based) utterances, which models must learn to handle.
key_idea: Collect 3,000+ free-form chat sessions in AI2-THOR between a human Commander with oracle task and world knowledge and a human Follower who acts in the environment, then derive three benchmarks from them: Execution from Dialogue History (EDH), Trajectory from Dialogue (TfD) and Two-Agent Task Completion (TATC).
insight: TEACh is much harder than ALFRED for ALFRED-style models. The adapted Episodic Transformer (E.T.) reaches only ~5–10% EDH success, versus 38.24% on ALFRED test-seen. A Vision-only ablation comes close to E.T.: E.T. is significantly better only on unseen splits, not on seen splits (Welch t-test with Bonferroni correction). So the model gets little purchase from the multi-speaker, phatic, anaphoric dialogue. Initializing from ALFRED-trained E.T. (+A, +S) gives small but non-significant gains. TfD, with ~130-action trajectories versus ~50 in ALFRED, is nearly unsolved (≤1.02% SR). Hand-crafted rule-based Commander/Follower agents took ~150 engineering hours and still reach 0% on four composite tasks. This shows planner-style solutions that work for ALFRED or VLN do not scale to TEACh's hierarchical tasks.
method: Data collection: two crowdworkers paired in AI2-THOR. The Commander sees the task via Progress Check, can run SearchObject (by string or by clicking an object instance), and has a top-down map and the Follower's view. The Follower is the only one who can act, using 16 actions (Forward/Backward/Turn L-R/Look Up-Down/Strafe L-R/Pickup/Place/Open/Close/ToggleOn/Off/Slice/Pour). They communicate only by free-form, non-turn-based text chat. Result: 3,320 successful sessions out of 4,365 (74.17% human success); 3,047 are used in the benchmark splits; 12 task types, 109 scenes, >45k utterances.
Interaction API: object manipulation takes an (x,y) click on the Follower's egocentric frame. The wrapper uses the GT segmentation mask to pick a valid object in a 10x10 pixel patch around the click.

Task Definition Language: a PDDL-like JSON spec built from components (conditions on object properties, determiners a/all/N, primary_condition, instance_shareable) and relations (parentReceptacles). It is hierarchical (tasks reference sub-tasks, e.g. Plate of Toast = Toast + Clean X) and parameterized (Put All X On Y). It checks task completion and generates templated Commander prompts.

Benchmarks: EDH segments sessions at dialogue acts. Given the dialogue plus action/image history, the agent predicts Follower actions until the next utterance and is scored on expected state changes (SR, GC, trajectory-length-weighted TLW). TfD asks for the whole session's Follower trajectory given the full dialogue. TATC asks for both Commander (with Progress Check) and Follower models, communicating via generated language. Splits follow ALFRED floorplans: train, val-seen/unseen, test-seen/unseen.

Adapted Episodic Transformer baseline: all history utterances are concatenated with separators as language input (no temporal alignment with actions). The ResNet-50 visual encoder and Mask R-CNN are pretrained on 325K ALFRED frames and kept frozen. Two multimodal transformer layers are followed by a new TEACh action head plus an object-class head. The predicted mask centroid becomes the click coordinate. Training uses cross-entropy on action and object class, AdamW, 20 epochs, batch size 3. Inference stops on Stop, at 1000 steps, or after 30 failed actions.

Ablations: history loss over all actions, not only future ones (H); initialization from ALFRED-trained E.T. (A) or ALFRED + synthetic-instruction E.T. (S); unimodal Lang-only and Vision-only baselines; a Random baseline.

Rule-based TATC agents (no learning): the Follower says 'What should I do next?' when its action queue is empty. The Commander then runs Progress Check, reads problem keys (7 types: parentReceptacle, isDirty, isFilledWithLiquid, isFilledWithCoffee, isBoiled, isCooked, Slice) and applies hand-crafted subgoal policies with a shortest-path planner. It emits templated low-level action strings with click coordinates.

setting.backbone: Episodic Transformer (E.T.): frozen ResNet-50 visual encoder + 2-layer multimodal transformer + language transformer, new TEACh action head, trained on TEACh from scratch or initialized from ALFRED E.T.; frozen Mask R-CNN (ALFRED-pretrained) for interaction masks. TATC uses hand-crafted rule-based Commander/Follower agents.
setting.training_data: TEACh train fold (1,482 sessions / 5,475 EDH instances). Visual encoder and Mask R-CNN pretrained on 325K ALFRED expert frames. Optional initialization from E.T. trained on ALFRED (A) or ALFRED + synthetic instructions (S).
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (900x900, resized to 224 for ResNet / 300 for Mask R-CNN) + concatenated dialogue history + past actions
setting.action_space: discrete navigation (Forward, Backward, Turn Left/Right, Look Up/Down, Strafe Left/Right) + object interactions (Pickup, Place, Open, Close, ToggleOn/Off, Slice, Pour) with (x,y) click on egocentric frame, plus Stop
setting.privileged: The benchmark API's click-to-object selection uses the simulator's GT segmentation mask (10x10 patch around the predicted coordinate); the learned E.T. Follower otherwise uses none. The rule-based TATC agents use oracle simulator state (Progress Check problem keys, object IDs, shortest-path planner).

numbers_note: All values are percentages; metric key TLW-SR/TLW-GC = the bracketed trajectory-length-weighted values. TEACh's seen test split has no allowed split label, so it is recorded as split 'test' with 'test-SEEN' stated in extra. Excluded variants +H+A and +H+S (Table 4): val-seen SR 8.39/9.38, val-unseen SR 6.12/5.7, test-seen SR 6.91/6.31, test-unseen SR 5.11/5.29. Appendix table gives per-task EDH SR breakdowns. TATC rule-based agents (Table 5) are not listed as entries because they were not evaluated on an official split. Their per-task rates match the counts over all 3,320 successful sessions (e.g. 47/176 = 26.70% for Water Plant); this is inferred, not stated. Results: Overall SR 24.40, 161.54±92.00 actions/session vs human 164.65±130.89; 0.00 on Boil, Toast, Sandwich, Breakfast. Paper notes the released split later filtered EDH instances, so numbers may differ from later leaderboard versions of TEACh.
results: The adapted E.T. Follower reaches 5.76/4.96 EDH SR on val-seen/val-unseen. The best variants reach 10.2 SR on val-seen (+A) and 7.83 SR on val-unseen (+S). All E.T. variants significantly beat Random and Lang-only, but beat Vision-only significantly only on unseen splits, and ALFRED initialization gains are not significant. This is far below E.T.'s 38.24% on ALFRED test-seen. TfD is nearly unsolved (SR ≤1.02). Rule-based TATC agents reach 24.40% overall success, around half on simple tasks, and 0–1.67% on composite tasks.
limitations: Only weak baselines: the E.T. adaptation concatenates the dialogue without speaker or temporal alignment to actions, is trained by teacher forcing on imperfect human trajectories, and drops ALFRED's subgoal-progress auxiliary losses. No learned Commander or TATC model is provided; TATC uses only oracle-based rule agents.

Object interaction relies on the simulator's GT segmentation in the click-to-object wrapper. Tasks are concentrated in kitchens with 12 task types, and evaluation is slow (up to ~14 h per unseen EDH split).
Benchmark versioning: EDH instances were refiltered in the released split, and test-split per-task information is not given, which complicates comparison with later papers.
